title: Questioning the evidence: says who, and how do they know?

summary.text: People can feel very sure and still be wrong. You will test this at home: ask your family questions about things in your own flat, ask how sure they are, and then go and check. Then you will learn three questions to ask about anything you hear: Says who? How do they know? Who is missing? They help you tell a claim that was checked from a story that only sounds true.
summary.art: A girl holding a clipboard in a kitchen, looking at a wall clock while her grandmother points at it, with a tick and a cross on the clipboard.

intro.hook: Kavya's aunt says, "Our wall clock has all twelve numbers on it. I see it every day." Kavya's uncle says, "No, it only has 12, 3, 6 and 9." Both of them are completely sure. They cannot both be right.
intro.text: Feeling sure did not settle it. Looking at the clock did. In this unit you find out how often people are sure and wrong, and how to check a claim before you believe it.
intro.art: A woman and a man in a living room both pointing confidently at a round wall clock that the viewer cannot quite see, with a girl between them looking up.

outcomes: I can say what a claim is, and what evidence is.
I can ask three questions about any claim: Says who? How do they know? Who is missing?
I can explain, using my own test, why being sure is not the same as being right.
I can tell a claim that someone checked from a story that only sounds true.
I can spot when evidence leaves people or things out, and say how that could change the answer.
I can explain why people remember the times a saying came true and forget the times it did not.
I can tell how Robert Wood showed in 1904 that the N-rays many scientists saw were not there.

terms.meaning: A sentence that says something is true. A claim can be right or wrong.
terms.example: "Our wall clock has all twelve numbers" is a claim. You can check it by looking.
terms.art: A speech bubble with the words 'Our clock has 12 numbers' next to a round wall clock.

terms.meaning: Something you can see, hear, count or measure that shows whether a claim is true.
terms.example: Looking at the clock and counting the numbers is evidence. Remembering the clock is not as good.
terms.art: A child's finger counting the numbers on a wall clock.

terms.meaning: Where a claim comes from: the person, book, message or place that said it.
terms.example: If a message says 'NASA says', the source should be NASA. You can check NASA's own website.
terms.art: A phone with a message on it, and an arrow pointing back to a person who wrote it.

terms.meaning: To look at the real thing, or ask someone who really knows, to see if a claim is true.
terms.example: Meenakshi checked how many steps go up to her floor by counting them as she climbed.
terms.art: A girl counting steps on a staircase in a block of flats, with numbers above each step.

terms.meaning: How certain a person feels about an answer. Being sure is a feeling. It is not evidence.
terms.example: Appa was very sure the gas stove had three burners. When he looked, it had four.
terms.art: A man with a confident smile next to a gas stove with four burners.

terms.meaning: The part of something that you look at, to learn about the whole thing.
terms.example: One spoonful from the top of a dal jar is a sample of the jar.
terms.art: A spoon taking dal from the top of a glass jar.

terms.meaning: The people or things that were left out of the evidence. Leaving them out can change the answer.
terms.example: If you ask only grown-ups whether the rasam is too spicy, the children's answer is missing.
terms.art: A family at a dining table, with the grown-ups answering a question and two children waiting to be asked.

terms.meaning: A story that many people repeat and believe, but that checking has shown to be wrong.
terms.example: Many people say a goldfish forgets everything in three seconds. Tests show goldfish remember things for months.
terms.art: A goldfish in a bowl swimming to the side where food is usually dropped.

explanations.definition: A claim says that something is true. Evidence is what you can see, count or measure that shows whether the claim is right.
explanations.description: Every day we hear claims. "It will rain today." "This soap kills germs." "The shop opens at nine." A claim on its own is just words. To know if it is true, we need evidence. The best evidence is something anyone can look at for themselves. If you say the shop opens at nine, the evidence is the board on its door, or going there at nine.
examples: Claim: our flat has seven windows. Evidence: walking round and counting them.
Claim: the milk has gone sour. Evidence: it smells sour and forms lumps when heated.
Claim: the tulsi plant leans towards the window. Evidence: a photo each day for a week.
explanations.art: A speech bubble saying 'Our flat has 7 windows', and a girl walking from window to window with a tally on paper.
explanations.context: This card says what a claim is and what evidence is.

explanations.concept: Being sure is not the same as being right
explanations.definition: How sure a person feels is a feeling inside them. It does not show whether their answer is true. Only checking shows that.
explanations.description: When we see something every day, we feel we know it well. But our memory keeps only the parts we need. In 2015, scientists in California asked 85 students to draw the Apple logo from memory, a picture they saw all the time. Only one student drew it with no mistakes. Most had felt sure they could do it. People who are very sure are often right, but not always. So when two sure people disagree, the way to settle it is to go and look.
examples: In the Sure or Right? test, someone may be very sure about the clock and still be wrong.
Two people can both be very sure and give different answers. At least one of them is wrong.
A person who says 'I'm not sure' and then checks often ends up knowing more than a person who is sure.
explanations.art: A boy drawing a clock from memory with numbers in the wrong places, beside the real clock on the wall.
explanations.context: This card explains what your Sure or Right? test showed: feeling sure does not make an answer right.

explanations.concept: Says who? Where a claim comes from
explanations.definition: The source of a claim is who said it, and how they came to say it. A good source is someone who looked, measured or tested for themselves.
explanations.description: Many claims reach us second-hand. A friend heard it from a cousin, who saw it in a message. Each time a claim is passed on, it can change, and the person passing it on usually has not checked it. So the first question is: says who? Then: did that person really say it? A message once went round the world saying that NASA had announced six days of darkness. NASA had said no such thing. Anyone could have checked NASA's own website.
examples: The weather office measures air, wind and clouds across India, so it is a good source for a rain forecast.
A doctor who has examined you is a better source about your cough than a message on a phone.
A famous name at the bottom of a message does not show that person wrote it.
explanations.art: A chain of people passing a message from phone to phone, with the words in the speech bubbles changing along the way.
explanations.context: This card is about the first of the three questions: says who?

explanations.concept: How do they know? Checked, or only sounds true
explanations.definition: A checked claim is one that someone tested, in a way others can repeat. A claim that only sounds true is repeated often, but nobody has shown it is right.
explanations.description: Some claims sound true because we hear them so often. "Lightning never strikes the same place twice." "A camel stores water in their hump." Both are wrong. Tall buildings are struck by lightning many times a year. A camel's hump is mostly fat. To ask 'how do they know?' is to ask what was done to find out. Did someone count, measure or test it? Could other people do the same and get the same answer? If nobody can say how it was found out, it is a story, even if it sounds true.
examples: Checked: an octopus has three hearts. Scientists have looked inside octopuses and seen them.
Only sounds true: we use only a tenth of our brain. Brain scans show every part of the brain is used during a day.
Checked at home: water from a tumbler left in the sun gets warm. You can feel it yourself.
explanations.art: Two boxes side by side: one labelled 'Checked' with a magnifying glass and a ruler, one labelled 'Only sounds true' with a cloud of speech bubbles.
explanations.context: This card is about the second question: how do they know?

explanations.concept: Who is missing? Evidence that leaves things out
explanations.definition: If evidence comes from only some people or some parts of a thing, the answer may be wrong for the rest. Asking 'who is missing?' finds the gaps.
explanations.description: Suppose you want to know if the rasam is too spicy. You ask Amma and Appa, and they say no. But nobody asked your little brother. His answer is missing, and it might be different. Scientists make this mistake too. For many years, most crash tests for cars used a dummy built to the size of an average man. Studies later found that women were more likely to be badly hurt in similar crashes. Women's bodies had been missing from the tests. Now some tests use dummies of other sizes too.
examples: In the Top-Spoon Test, a spoonful from the top of the jar left out the moong at the bottom.
A survey of only the children in a building cannot say what the grandparents think.
For many years, many new medicines were tested mostly on men, so less was known about how they worked for women.
explanations.art: A crash-test dummy the size of a man sitting in a car seat, with a smaller dummy waiting outside the car.
explanations.context: This card is about the third question: who is missing?

explanations.concept: Why we remember the hits and forget the misses
explanations.definition: People tend to notice and remember the times a saying came true, and forget the times it did not. Scientists call this confirmation bias.
explanations.description: A day when a guest arrives is easy to remember. A day when nothing happens is easy to forget. So if you believe that a cawing crow brings a guest, you remember every time it worked. The many mornings when the crow cawed and nobody came slip away. The saying seems to come true again and again. The fix is to write down every time, the hits and the misses, and then count both.
examples: Meenakshi's Paati remembered four guests on crow days, and forgot nine crow days with no guest.
Someone who thinks Fridays are unlucky remembers the bad Fridays and forgets the good ones.
A tally kept every day remembers the misses for you.
explanations.art: A tally chart on a fridge door with two rows, 'Crow cawed, guest came' and 'Crow cawed, no guest', the second row much longer.
explanations.context: This card explains why some sayings feel true even when they are not.

explanations.description: Thinkers have argued for a long time about what makes something science and not just a story. Most agree that science needs evidence that others can check. They disagree about what matters most.
examples: "A crow cawing brings a guest" can be tested with a tally. If guests came no more often on crow days, the claim fails.
"Everything happens for a reason" is hard to test, because any result could fit it.

perspectives.explanation: A claim is scientific if a test could show it is wrong. 'The crow brings guests' is scientific, because a tally could show it fails. A claim that fits every possible result tells us nothing about the world.

perspectives.who: Thomas Kuhn, a historian of science (1922 to 1996)
perspectives.explanation: Scientists work inside a shared way of seeing. They do not drop an idea after one failed test. They often keep it until a better idea comes along.
What matters most is that a claim is checked again and again, by different people in different places, and that they share how they did it so others can try.

explanations.art: Three people at a table arguing politely over a notebook with a tally chart in it.
explanations.context: This card is about a question thinkers still argue over: what makes something science?

explanations.description: Nobody can test every claim. You have not been to the Moon, and you have not looked inside an octopus. So we all trust other people. 'Says who?' does not mean 'trust nobody'. It means trust people because of how they know, not because of how sure they sound. A good source can say how they found out, lets others check, and changes their mind when new evidence comes. People still argue about how much to trust experts, and when.
examples: You trust the train timetable because the railway sets the times and you can see trains leave on time.
You trust that the Earth goes round the Sun because many people, over hundreds of years, measured it in ways anyone can repeat.
explanations.art: A girl reading a railway timetable at a station in Chennai while a train pulls in on time.
explanations.context: This card says why asking 'says who?' does not mean trusting nobody.

agreed.text: Being sure about an answer does not make it right. Checking is what shows whether it is right.
agreed.evidence: In many studies, people who felt sure about everyday things they had seen many times, such as a logo or a coin, still made mistakes when they drew or picked them.

agreed.text: People remember the times a belief came true more than the times it did not.
agreed.evidence: Psychologists have shown this many times, by asking people to recall events and then comparing their memory with a written record.

agreed.text: A claim is more trustworthy when other people can repeat the test and get the same result.
agreed.evidence: N-rays were seen in one lab and its followers, but careful tests elsewhere found nothing. Real discoveries, like X-rays, were seen by everyone who repeated the test.

agreed.text: Evidence that leaves out a group can give the wrong answer for that group.
agreed.evidence: Crash tests built around an average man's body missed injuries that women were more likely to get.

challenging.claim: If very many people believe something, it must be true.
challenging.for: Many things that most people believe are true, such as the Earth being round.
challenging.against: Many people once believed in N-rays, and many still believe that lightning never strikes twice. The number of believers is not evidence. What counts is whether the claim was checked.
challenging.context: This card is about a common idea: if many people believe it, it must be true.

challenging.claim: Old sayings and home remedies are just stories.
challenging.who: Some people who trust only modern science
challenging.for: Many old sayings, like the crow and the guest, fail when they are tested.
challenging.against: Some old knowledge passes the test. Tu Youyou, a scientist in China, found a malaria medicine in sweet wormwood after reading a treatment in a book about 1,700 years old. The fair answer is to test each one.
challenging.context: This card is about the opposite mistake: deciding without checking that old knowledge is always wrong.

challenging.for: Science has ways to catch mistakes, such as repeating tests.
challenging.against: In 1903 and 1904, many scientists in France reported N-rays, which did not exist. They saw what they expected to see. Science caught the mistake only when someone tested it in a way that could fail.
challenging.context: This card is about whether scientists can be fooled too.

challenging.for: Experts have studied a subject for years, and are right far more often than people who have not.
challenging.against: Experts can be wrong, and they sometimes disagree. Most people say we should trust an expert who can explain how they know and who changes their mind when the evidence changes.
challenging.context: This card is about a real argument: how much should we trust experts?

big_questions.q: Your family member was very sure, and wrong. What was the feeling of being sure made of, if it was not made of knowing?
big_questions.hint: Think about where the answer came from: the clock, or their memory of the clock.

big_questions.q: Is there anything you can be completely sure about without checking?
big_questions.hint: What about the fact that you are thinking right now?

big_questions.q: Most of what you know, you were told. How much of it have you checked yourself?
big_questions.hint: Try a few: the Earth is round, your birthday, the name of your great-grandmother.

big_questions.q: When a whole group is missing from the evidence, who decides that they should be included?
big_questions.hint: Think of the crash-test dummy. Who noticed women were missing?

big_questions.q: If a saying is not true, why do people keep passing it on?
big_questions.hint: Paati kept feeding the crows. Does a saying do other things for people, apart from being true?

story.title: Paati's Crow
story.note: The story is made up. The science in it is true: people remember the times a saying came true and forget the times it did not, and a written tally of every day shows both. House crows are found in almost every Indian city, and they call to each other often, most of all where food is put out.
text: Every morning in Madurai, Paati put a small heap of cooked rice on the balcony rail. Every morning, a crow came. Often two or three came. They hopped along the rail, pecked at the rice and called out loudly, kaa, kaa.
One Saturday a crow called for a long time. Paati looked up from her coffee and smiled. "Someone is coming today," she said. "When the crow calls like that, a guest always comes."
Meenakshi was nine. She put down her dosa. "Always, Paati?"
"Always," said Paati. "Last month the crow called, and your Chitti came from Trichy with a box of sweets. Before that, the crow called, and Mrs. Iyer from the third floor came to borrow curd."
That evening, Meenakshi's school friend Revathi came over with her mother. Paati gave Meenakshi a look that said, you see?

Meenakshi thought about it in bed. Paati remembered the days a guest came. But did she remember the other days? Meenakshi could not remember them herself. A day with no guest was just an ordinary day. Nobody talks about an ordinary day.

The next morning she found an old notebook. She drew a table with three columns: the date, "Did the crow call?" and "Did a guest come?" Her brother Arun, who was six, wanted to help. "I'll be the crow watcher," he said. "You be the guest watcher."
"We have to write every day," said Meenakshi. "Even the boring days. Especially the boring days."
"Why the boring days?" asked Arun.
"Because those are the days everyone forgets."
Paati heard them and laughed. "Write all you like," she said. "The crow knows what they are doing."

For two weeks they wrote. Arun stood at the balcony door every morning while Paati put out the rice. He wrote a big red tick if a crow called. A crow called on Monday, and on Tuesday, and on every day that week. On the second Tuesday it rained hard, and no crow came. Meenakshi wrote a cross. Every other morning, the crows came and called.

Meenakshi watched the door. A guest counted only if they were not family who lived in the flat. The milkman did not count, because he came every day. On Wednesday, Mrs. Iyer came for curd again. On Friday, Revathi came back to do homework with Meenakshi. On the first Saturday, Chitti phoned, but did not come. The phone call did not count either. On the second Sunday, two cousins came for lunch. On the second Thursday, a neighbour came with a wedding invitation.
At the end of the two weeks, Meenakshi and Arun sat on the floor with Paati and the notebook. They counted together.
The crow had called on 13 mornings. A guest had come on 4 of those days.
"Four!" said Paati, pleased. "Four guests, all on crow days. What did I tell you?"
"But Paati," said Meenakshi, "look at the other line. On 9 days the crow called and nobody came."
Paati put on her glasses and looked. She looked for a long time. "Nine," she said. "I don't remember those days at all."
"That's the point," said Meenakshi. "Nobody remembers them. You remembered the four days a guest came, because a guest is special. The nine ordinary days just went away."
Arun had a question. "What about the day with no crow? Did a guest come then?"
"No," said Meenakshi. "But that was only one day, and it was raining hard. Who visits in heavy rain? One day isn't enough to tell us anything."
Paati was quiet. Then she said something Meenakshi had not thought of. "Do you know why the crows call so much on our balcony?"
Meenakshi shook her head.

"Because I put out rice," said Paati. "When one crow finds food, they call, and the others come. I make them call, every single morning. Of course the crow calls on guest days. The crow calls on every day."
Meenakshi stared at her. Paati had found the biggest problem with the saying herself. If the crow called every morning, then the crow could never tell them which mornings were special.
"So the saying is wrong?" asked Arun, a little sad.
"The saying is wrong," said Paati. "Your sister checked it, and the notebook shows it." She stood up and fetched the rice pot. "But I will still feed the crows. They are my friends, not my postmen."

The next morning the crow called on the balcony rail, kaa, kaa. Arun looked at Meenakshi. Meenakshi looked at Paati. Paati smiled and said, "Someone may come today, and someone may not. Let's write it down."
story.epiphany: For the parent: Paati remembered the hits (crow days with a guest) and forgot the misses (crow days with no guest). That is confirmation bias. Writing down every day, the boring ones too, put the misses back. Paati then found a second problem: the crow called every day, because she fed them, so a crow call could not pick out guest days. A saying can only be tested if there are days when the sign is missing, to compare with.
ask: Why was Paati so sure the crow brought guests?
Why did Meenakshi say they must write down the boring days too?
On how many crow days did nobody come? Why had Paati forgotten them?
Why was one rainy day with no crow not enough to tell them anything?
What did Paati notice about why the crows called every morning?

games.title: Checked or Only Sounds True? a card game
games.context: This is a card game about claims. A player reads a claim card. Everyone decides: has someone checked it and found it true, or does it only sound true? Then you say how someone could find out.

printables.title: 16 claim cards
items: A goldfish forgets everything after three seconds. (Only sounds true. Scientists have trained goldfish to come to a sound at feeding time, and they remembered it for months.)
An octopus has three hearts. (Checked. Scientists have looked inside octopuses: two hearts pump blood to the gills and one to the rest of the body.)
Lightning never strikes the same place twice. (Only sounds true. Very tall buildings are struck by lightning many times every year.)
A camel stores water in their hump. (Only sounds true. The hump is mostly fat. A camel uses it when food is short.)
Your heart beats faster when you run. (Checked. Count your pulse for 15 seconds before and after running on the spot, and see.)
Bulls charge at a red cloth because they hate red. (Only sounds true. Bulls cannot tell red from green well. In tests, they charged at a moving cloth whatever its colour.)
An ostrich buries their head in the sand to hide. (Only sounds true. Ostriches lower their heads to turn their eggs in a nest in the ground. From far away, it can look like they are hiding.)
We use only one tenth of our brain. (Only sounds true. Brain scans show that every part of the brain is busy at some time during a day.)
The Moon makes its own light. (Only sounds true. The Moon shines with sunlight bouncing off it. That is why we see only the lit part.)
A crow can remember a person's face. (Checked. In the USA, scientists wore a mask while they caught and ringed crows. For years after, crows scolded anyone wearing that mask.)
Plants grow towards light. (Checked. Put a potted plant by a window for a week. The shoots lean towards the window.)
Swallowed chewing gum stays in your stomach for seven years. (Only sounds true. It passes through the body in a few days, like other things the body does not digest.)
Bats are blind. (Only sounds true. Bats can see. Many kinds also find their way in the dark by listening to echoes.)
Water boils at a lower temperature high up on a mountain. (Checked. Climbers have measured it with thermometers many times.)
Wild snakes drink milk. (Only sounds true. Wild snakes eat animals such as rats, frogs and eggs, and drink water.)
Sound cannot travel through empty space. (Checked. A bell ringing inside a jar goes quiet when the air is pumped out of the jar.)

check.q: Many people say a goldfish forgets everything after three seconds. Scientists trained goldfish to come to a sound at feeding time. Months later, the fish still came. What does this show?
options: Goldfish remember for much longer than three seconds
check.why: The fish remembered the sound for months. The three-second story is repeated a lot, but the test shows it is wrong.

flow.do: Play the rest of the cards. Take turns to read. Give points as in the rules.
flow.say: Now tell me how someone could find out. That's where the extra point is.
flow.kid: Hold up your card. Then say how someone could find out.

ask.q: How could someone find out if bats are blind?
good: Test whether bats react to light or to things they can see.
Watch bats with a camera in the dark and in the light.

flow.parent: The 'how could we find out' part matters more than the card. Some claims sound strange and are true, like the octopus. Some sound sensible and are wrong, like the camel.

flow.do: Add up the points. Ask which card surprised your child most.
flow.say: Which claim surprised you most? Had you believed it before today?
flow.kid: Which card surprised you most? Did you believe it before?

games.title: Who Would Know? a source-picking game
games.context: This is a quick game about sources. Each card has a claim and two people or places who might know. You pick the better source and say why.

printables.title: 8 source cards
items: 'It will rain in Chennai tomorrow.' Who would know better: a neighbour whose knee aches before rain, or the weather office? (The weather office. It measures air, wind and clouds across the country every day.)
'The train to Madurai leaves at 6:15.' Who would know better: a friend who went last year, or the railway timetable for today? (The timetable. Times can change, and the railway sets them.)
'Paati's favourite festival is Pongal.' Who would know better: a cousin, or Paati? (Paati. Only she knows what she likes best.)
'This cut needs stitches.' Who would know better: a message on a phone, or a doctor who looks at the cut? (The doctor. She has seen the cut and is trained to judge it.)
'Our flat has seven windows.' Who would know better: Appa's memory, or counting them now? (Counting them now. Memory can be wrong, as the Sure or Right? test showed.)
'The match yesterday ended in a draw.' Who would know better: a friend who heard it from a friend, or the scorecard? (The scorecard. It was written as the match was played.)
'This medicine is safe for children.' Who would know better: an advert, or a doctor and the tests the medicine went through? (The doctor and the tests. An advert is trying to sell.)
'Crows were calling on our balcony this morning.' Who would know better: a guess, or the tally you wrote this morning? (The tally. It was written at the time.)

rules: Turn over a source card and read the claim and the two sources.
Say why it is better: did they see it, measure it, or write it down at the time?
One point for the source, one for the reason.

flow.do: Read the first card, the rain in Chennai, aloud.
flow.say: Who would know better if it will rain tomorrow: a neighbour whose knee aches, or the weather office? Why?
flow.kid: Who would know better about rain: the knee, or the weather office?
flow.context: This is the start of Who Would Know?, a game about choosing a good source.

check.q: Who would know better whether it will rain in Chennai tomorrow?
options: A neighbour whose knee aches before rain
The weather office, which measures air, wind and clouds every day
check.why: The weather office measures the air across India and keeps records of what came next. That is how they know. A knee feels only one place, and nobody has kept a record of how often it is right.

flow.do: Go through the other cards. Let your child pick and give a reason before you read the answer.
flow.say: Which is the better source? Did they see it, measure it, or write it down at the time?
flow.kid: Pick the better source. Did they see it, or measure it?

ask.q: Why is Paati the best source about her favourite festival?
good: Because only Paati knows what she likes.
Because it is about her own feelings.

flow.parent: Notice that the best source changes with the claim. For the weather, it is the people who measure. For Paati's favourite festival, it is Paati herself.

flow.do: Ask what all the good sources had in common.
flow.say: What did all the good sources have in common?
flow.kid: What was the same about all the good sources?

experiments.title: Sure or Right? The Family Check
experiments.context: In this experiment you ask your family questions about things in your own flat. Each person also says how sure they are. Then you go and check every answer. You find out whether the very sure answers are always right.
experiments.question: When people are very sure about something in their own home, are they always right?
experiments.predict: Think of the grown-ups in your home. When they say 'I'm very sure', will they always be right? Will a 'just guessing' answer ever be right? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Everyone gets the same questions, in the same words, read the same way. Nobody may look at the thing or go to it before answering. Each person answers alone, out of earshot of the others, so nobody copies. Each person says how sure they are before anyone checks. We check every answer by looking at the real thing, in the same way for everyone.
results_table: How sure (very sure, a bit sure, just guessing)

materials.item: a notebook and a pencil
a ruler, to draw the table
two or more people to ask: family at home, or relatives on a phone call about their own home
three coloured pencils or crayons: green for very sure, yellow for a bit sure, red for just guessing

experiments.safety: Count the stairs only with a grown-up, and walk, don't run. Don't open the fridge or the gas stove to check. Look from where you stand.

schedule.what: Choose 8 questions, draw the table, ask each person, check every answer, and count.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then count three numbers for each colour: how many answers were given, how many were right, how many were wrong. Write them in a small box at the bottom of the page.

flow.do: 1. Read out the list of question ideas in the note below. 2. Your child picks 8 that can be checked in your home. 3. Write them down the side of the page.
flow.say: We are going to ask the family questions about our own home. Pick questions we can check by looking.
flow.kid: Pick 8 questions about your home. Each one must be easy to check.
flow.context: This is the first step of Sure or Right? You choose questions about your own home that you can check.
flow.parent: Question ideas: How many numbers are written on our wall clock? How many windows does our flat have? How many burners does our gas stove have? Which way does the kitchen tap turn to open, like a clock's hands or the other way? What colour is the cap of the toothpaste? How many steps go up from the ground to our floor? Which hand does Amma wear her watch on? What is the first word printed on the milk packet? Mix a few easy ones with a few hard ones.

flow.do: Help your child draw the results table with a ruler. Then ask for a prediction and a reason.
flow.say: Before we ask anyone: do you think the very sure answers will all be right? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Will the very sure answers all be right? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Will the very sure answers all be right? Why?
good: Yes, because people know their own home.
No, because people don't look closely at things they see every day.
Most will be right, but maybe one will be wrong.

flow.parent: Write the guess and the reason at the top of the page. Do not say what you expect. Any guess with a reason is a good start.

flow.do: 1. Your child asks each person the 8 questions, one person at a time, in another room from the others. 2. After each answer, your child asks: very sure, a bit sure, or just guessing? 3. Your child writes the answer and colours the sure box.
flow.say: Ask each question in the same words. After each answer, ask how sure they are. Don't tell them if they are right.
flow.kid: Ask each person alone. Say each question the same way. Then ask: how sure are you? Colour green, yellow or red.
flow.parent: Answer the questions yourself too, honestly, without looking. Nobody may walk to the clock or the tap before answering. If only one grown-up is at home, phone a relative and ask about their own home, and they check while you wait on the phone.

flow.do: Now go round the home together and check every answer. Count the windows, look at the clock, turn the tap. Mark each answer right or wrong.
flow.say: Now we find out. Let's go and look at each thing. Was the answer right or wrong?
flow.kid: Now go and look at each thing. Was each answer right or wrong?

check.q: Appa was very sure the clock has all 12 numbers. How do we find out if he is right?
options: Ask who is the oldest in the family
check.why: Only the clock can show what is on the clock. Asking again only tells us what Appa remembers. Age does not make a memory right.

flow.do: 1. Count the green answers, and how many of them were wrong. Do the same for yellow and red. 2. Ask your child for a claim, the evidence and a reason. 3. Then read the card 'Being sure is not the same as being right'.
flow.say: What did you find out? What did you see that shows it? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Count each colour. How many were wrong? What did you find out?

ask.q: Were all the very sure answers right?
good: No. Two green answers were wrong.
Most green answers were right, but Paati was very sure about the windows and got it wrong.

ask.q: Why might someone be sure and wrong about their own home?
good: They see it every day but don't look closely.
They remember it wrong.
They remember an old clock, not this one.

flow.parent: Most families find at least one very sure answer that is wrong. Often the very sure answers are right more often than the guesses, and that is worth noticing too. If every green answer was right, ask: did we pick only easy questions? Try three harder ones, such as the steps or the tap.

experiments.title: The Top-Spoon Test: does one spoonful tell you about the whole jar?
experiments.context: In this experiment you fill a jar with two kinds of dal in layers. You take a spoonful from the top and decide what is in the jar. Then you look again. It shows what goes wrong when part of the evidence is missing.
experiments.question: Does a spoonful from the top of a jar show what the whole jar holds?
experiments.predict: If you take one spoonful from the top of the jar, will it show both kinds of dal? What about after the jar is shaken? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: The thing we change: where the sample comes from, and whether the jar was mixed. The things we keep the same: the same jar, the same spoon, a level spoonful each time. What we count: how many grains of each kind are in each spoonful.
results_table: What this sample says the jar holds

materials.item: a clear glass or plastic jar, or a tall clear tumbler
about 1 cup of a big pale dal or grain, such as chana or white rice
about 1 cup of a small dark grain, such as green moong, rajma or black mustard seeds
a teaspoon
a steel plate, to tip each spoonful onto
a cloth or a sheet of newspaper, to wrap round the jar

experiments.safety: Do this away from small children who might put grains in their mouth or nose. Put the grains back into their tins afterwards.

schedule.what: Fill the jar in layers, take a spoonful from the top, then mix and take three more, and count.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw the jar as it looked before mixing and after mixing.

flow.do: 1. Out of your child's sight, pour the moong into the jar first, then the chana on top. 2. Wrap the cloth round the jar so the sides can't be seen. 3. Put the jar on the table.
flow.say: This jar has dal in it. You can only see the top. Take one spoonful and tell me what's in the jar.
flow.kid: You can only see the top of this jar. Take one spoonful.
flow.context: This is the start of the Top-Spoon Test. A jar holds two kinds of dal, but you can only see the top.
flow.parent: Pour gently so the layers stay separate. A layer of at least 3 centimetres of each works well.

flow.do: Your child takes one level spoonful from the top, tips it on the plate and counts each kind. Write the numbers in the table.
flow.say: Count the grains of each kind. What does this spoonful say is in the jar?
flow.kid: Count each kind. What does the spoonful say is in the jar?

ask.q: What is in the jar, going by this spoonful?
good: Only chana.
All chana, no moong.

flow.do: Take off the cloth. Look at the jar from the side together.
flow.say: Now look at the whole jar. Was the spoonful right about the jar?
flow.kid: Look at the jar from the side. Was the spoonful right?

check.q: The top spoonful had only chana. Why was it wrong about the jar?
options: The moong at the bottom was missing from the sample
check.why: The sample came only from the top, so the moong at the bottom was left out. A sample tells you only about the part it came from.

flow.do: 1. Tip everything onto a big plate, mix it well with clean hands, and pour it back into the jar. 2. Take three spoonfuls from three places: the top, the middle and near the bottom. 3. Count each one and write the numbers.
flow.say: Now the dal is mixed. Take three spoonfuls from three places. Do they agree with each other now?
flow.kid: Mix the dal. Take three spoonfuls from three places. Count each.

ask.q: What do the three spoonfuls say now?
good: They all have both kinds.
They have some of each, but not exactly the same numbers.

flow.parent: Mixing by hand works better than shaking. When a jar is shaken, big grains tend to rise to the top again. If your three samples disagree, that is worth talking about. It shows why scientists take samples from many places.

flow.do: Ask for a claim, the evidence and a reason.
flow.say: What did you find out about taking one spoonful from the top?
flow.kid: What did you find out? What did you see?
flow.think: Where else might someone take a sample from only the top, and get the wrong answer?

activities.title: One True, One Made Up
activities.context: This is a quick start to the unit. A grown-up says two surprising facts in the same sure voice. One is true and one is made up. You have to decide how you could find out which is which.

materials.item: nothing, just two people

schedule.what: Hear two claims, pick the true one, and say how you could check.

activities.record: Write the two claims. Under each, write one way to check it.

flow.do: Say both claims in exactly the same sure voice, with a straight face.
flow.say: Here are two facts. An octopus has three hearts. A crow can count up to one hundred. One is true and one I made up. Which one is true?
flow.kid: Listen to two facts. One is true. One is made up. Which is true?
flow.context: This is the start of the unit on questioning the evidence. You hear two claims said in the same sure voice.

ask.q: Which one is true? Why do you think so?
good: The octopus one, because I've heard it before.
I can't tell, you said them both the same way.

flow.parent: The octopus claim is true: an octopus has two hearts that pump blood to the gills and one for the rest of the body. The crow claim is made up. Don't say which is true yet.

flow.do: Ask how your child could find out, without asking you.
flow.say: I said them both the same way, so my voice can't help you. How could you find out which one is true, without asking me?
flow.kid: The voice was the same. How could you find out which is true?

good: Look it up in a book about animals.
Ask someone who studies octopuses.
Find out how scientists know.

flow.do: Tell your child which was true. Then try one more pair: 'A camel stores water in their hump' and 'Your heart beats faster when you run.'
flow.say: The octopus one is true. Scientists have looked inside octopuses and counted. Now, a camel stores water in their hump, or your heart beats faster when you run. Which can you check right now?
flow.kid: Which one can you check yourself, right now?

check.q: A grown-up says two facts in the same sure voice. What helps you decide which one is true?
check.why: Both facts were said in the same sure voice, so the voice tells you nothing. You need evidence. You can check the heartbeat by feeling your pulse before and after running. The camel's hump is mostly fat, not water.

activities.title: Three Questions on a Message
activities.context: In this activity you read made-up messages, like the ones people forward on their phones. For each one, you ask three questions: Says who? How do they know? Who is missing?

materials.item: the 5 message cards below, written or printed on paper
a pencil

schedule.what: Read five messages and ask the three questions about each.

activities.record: For each message, write the answer to one of the three questions.

flow.do: Write the three questions on a card where your child can see them: Says who? How do they know? Who is missing?
flow.say: Here are three questions we can ask about anything we hear. Says who? How do they know? Who is missing?
flow.kid: Here are three questions. Says who? How do they know? Who is missing?
flow.context: This is the start of Three Questions on a Message. You learn three questions to ask about any claim.

flow.do: Read each message card. After each, your child picks the question that shows the biggest problem with it. The message cards: 1. 'Scientists say this cream makes everyone's skin glow.' 2. 'NASA says the Earth will go dark for six days next month. Forward to everyone!' 3. 'I asked my three best friends and they all love cricket. So every child loves cricket.' 4. 'My uncle tried this tea once and his cold went away the next day. It cures colds!' 5. 'The weather office says heavy rain is likely in Chennai tomorrow.'
flow.say: Here is a message. Which of the three questions shows what's wrong with it? Or is this one a good source?
flow.kid: Read the message. Which question shows what is wrong?

ask.q: What is wrong with the cricket message?
good: Who is missing: only three friends were asked.
Children who don't like cricket were not asked.

ask.q: What is wrong with the tea message?
good: How do they know? Colds often go away by themselves in a few days.
He only tried it once.

flow.parent: Good answers: 1. Says who? Which scientists? 2. Says who? Did NASA say it? Check NASA's own website. A message like this did spread round the world, and NASA had never said it. 3. Who is missing? Only three friends were asked. 4. How do they know? Most colds go away in a few days anyway, so one try shows nothing. 5. This is a good source. The weather office measures the air and clouds every day.

flow.do: Ask which message your child would trust most, and why.
flow.say: Which message would you trust most? Why?
flow.kid: Which message would you trust most? Why?

check.q: Nila's uncle drank a herbal tea once, and his cold went away the next day. What is the biggest problem with saying the tea cures colds?
options: Tea is too hot to drink
Colds often go away by themselves, so one try shows nothing
Her uncle is not a scientist
check.why: Most colds get better in a few days anyway. To know if the tea helped, you would need to compare many people who drank it with many who did not.

activities.title: Be Clever Hans: the horse who read faces
activities.context: About 1904, a horse in Berlin called Hans was famous for tapping out answers to sums with a hoof. In 1907, a scientist called Oskar Pfungst found that Hans watched the face and body of the person asking. In this activity you play Hans and find out how.

materials.item: a steel spoon and a steel plate, to tap
small slips of paper with easy sums, such as 2 + 3, and a pencil
a third person, if you can: another family member to pick the sums

schedule.what: Play Hans twice: once when the asker knows the answer, once when nobody watching does.

activities.record: Write how many sums you got right each round.

flow.do: Tell the story of Clever Hans in a few words, using the context above.
flow.say: Hans was a horse in Berlin. People asked him sums, and he tapped his hoof the right number of times. Many experts were fooled. How do you think he did it?
flow.kid: Hans was a horse who tapped out answers to sums. How did he do it?
flow.context: This is the start of Be Clever Hans. You hear about a horse who seemed to do sums.

flow.do: Round 1: You know the answer. Your child taps the spoon on the plate slowly and must stop at the right number without counting. As your child nears the answer, let your body relax a little, and lean back slightly at the right number.
flow.say: Don't count. Just tap slowly and watch me. Stop when you think it's right. Here's the first: 2 plus 3.
flow.kid: Don't count. Tap slowly. Watch the grown-up's face. Stop when it feels right.
flow.parent: Pfungst found that questioners leaned forward while Hans tapped, and moved very slightly when he reached the answer, without meaning to. You do it on purpose here. Do five sums.

flow.do: Round 2: Someone else picks the sum slip and shows it only to your child. You watch, but you don't know the answer. Your child again taps without counting.
flow.say: This time I don't know the answer. Tap and watch me, and stop when it feels right.
flow.kid: The grown-up doesn't know the answer now. Tap and watch. What happens?
flow.parent: If there is no third person, put the sum slips face down, shuffle them, and let your child pick one without looking. Neither of you knows the answer.

flow.do: Compare the two rounds.
flow.say: When did you get more right? Why?
flow.kid: Which round did you get more right? Why?

check.q: Clever Hans got sums right when the person asking knew the answer. He got them wrong when nobody watching knew. What does that show?
options: Hans was doing the sums in his head
Hans was reading tiny signs from the person asking
check.why: If Hans were doing the sums, it would not matter who knew the answer. He was very good at reading faces and bodies, a real skill, but he was not doing the sums. Pfungst found this by testing when the asker did not know.

activities.title: Who Did We Leave Out? The Spice Survey
activities.context: In this activity you ask some people a question, then ask more people, and see if the answer changes. It shows how leaving people out can change what the evidence says.

materials.item: a notebook and a pencil
as many people as you can reach: family at home, and relatives or neighbours on the phone

activities.safety: Ask neighbours only with a grown-up beside you.

schedule.what: Ask the grown-ups first, then everyone, and compare.

activities.record: Two tally charts: 'Grown-ups only' and 'Everyone'. Write one sentence on whether the answer changed.

flow.do: Your child asks only the grown-ups: 'Should our rasam be more spicy, less spicy or the same?' Make a tally.
flow.say: First ask only the grown-ups. Should our rasam be more spicy, less spicy or the same?
flow.kid: Ask only the grown-ups first. More spicy, less spicy or the same?
flow.context: This is the start of the Spice Survey. You ask a question to only some people first.

flow.do: Now your child asks everyone else too: children, grandparents, anyone on a phone call. Make a second tally that includes everyone.
flow.say: Now ask everyone else too. Who did we leave out the first time?
flow.kid: Now ask everyone, children too. Who did you leave out before?
flow.parent: Any other question works if your family doesn't eat rasam: the best time for dinner, or how loud the TV should be.

flow.do: Compare the two tallies.
flow.say: Did the answer change when everyone was asked? Whose answer was missing before?
flow.kid: Did the answer change? Whose answer was missing?

check.q: Lakshmi asked only her parents if the rasam was too spicy. Both said no. What is the problem with saying 'Nobody thinks it's too spicy'?
options: The children, and anyone else not asked, are missing
check.why: Only two people were asked. The children might find it too spicy. To say what 'everybody' thinks, you have to ask everybody, or at least people from every group.

activities.title: The Passing Message
activities.context: In this activity a message is whispered from person to person. At the end you compare it with the first message. It shows why a claim you hear second-hand is weaker evidence than a claim from someone who was there.

materials.item: 4 or more people, or 2 people and a phone call with relatives
a slip of paper with a message written on it

schedule.what: Pass a whispered message along and compare the first and last.

activities.record: Write the first message and the last message one under the other. Circle what changed.

flow.do: Write a message on a slip of paper and fold it. Try this one: 'On Tuesday Divya saw two green parrots eating guava at seven.' Whisper it once to the first person.
flow.say: I'm going to whisper a message once. Whisper it once to the next person. No repeating.
flow.kid: Listen to the whisper. Whisper it once to the next person.
flow.context: This is the start of The Passing Message. A message is whispered from person to person.

flow.do: The message goes along the line. The last person says it out loud. Then open the paper and read the first message.
flow.say: Last person, say it out loud. Now let's read what I first wrote.
flow.kid: Say the message out loud. Now read the paper. What changed?
flow.parent: With only two people at home, whisper it to your child, who tells it to a relative on the phone, who tells it back after a few minutes of other chat.

flow.do: Talk about who you would trust most to say what happened.
flow.say: If you wanted to know what really happened on Tuesday, who would you ask?
flow.kid: Who would you ask to know what really happened?

check.q: A message went along five people and changed. Whose words are the best evidence of what happened?
options: The person who saw it and wrote it down
check.why: Every time a message is passed on, it can change. The person who saw it, and wrote it down at the time, is the closest to what really happened.

projects.title: The Crow and Guest Week: test a saying
projects.context: In this 7-day project you test a saying, like Meenakshi in the story Paati's Crow. Every day you write down two things: did a crow call near your home in the morning, and did a guest come? At the end you count the hits and the misses.

materials.item: a notebook and a pencil, or a sheet stuck on the fridge
a window or a balcony where you can hear or see crows

projects.safety: Watch from inside the window or the balcony door. Don't lean out over a balcony rail.

schedule.what: Choose the saying. Decide what counts as a guest and what counts as a crow calling. Draw the table and fill in day 1.
Fill in the last day, count the four boxes, and tell the family what you found.

projects.record: A table with one row per day: date, crow called (yes or no), guest came (yes or no). At the end, a box with four counts: crow and guest, crow and no guest, no crow and guest, no crow and no guest.

flow.do: 1. Choose the saying to test. The crow one works in most Indian cities. 2. Agree on the rules: what is a guest, and what counts as the crow calling. 3. Draw the table. 4. Fill in today.
flow.say: Many people say a calling crow means a guest is coming. Let's test it for a week. First, what counts as a guest?
flow.kid: We will test a saying for a week. What counts as a guest?
flow.context: This is day 1 of the Crow and Guest Week. You set up a test of a saying.

ask.q: What should count as a guest?
good: Someone who doesn't live here.
Not the milkman, because he comes every day.
Not a phone call.

flow.parent: Deciding the rules first is important. If you decide afterwards, it is easy to count things that fit the saying. If your family has a different saying, such as 'an itchy palm means money is coming', test that instead.

flow.do: Each day, your child fills in the row: did a crow call in the morning, and did a guest come?
flow.say: Did a crow call this morning? Did anyone visit today? Write it down, even if nothing happened.
flow.kid: Did a crow call? Did a guest come? Write it, even boring days.
flow.wait: Do this once a day for 7 days, at bedtime.
flow.parent: The boring days, with no guest, are the most important rows. They are the ones people forget.

flow.do: 1. On day 7, count the four boxes. 2. Your child tells the family what they found, with the table as evidence.
flow.say: Count the days the crow called and a guest came. Now count the days the crow called and nobody came. What does the table show?
flow.kid: Count the four boxes. What does your table show?
flow.wait: Day 7: count and tell the family.

check.q: In Divya's week, a crow called on all 7 mornings and a guest came on 2 days. Does the crow bring guests?
options: Yes, because guests came on crow days
We can't tell, because the crow called every day, so there are no quiet days to compare
check.why: If the crow calls every morning, every guest will arrive on a crow day, whatever brings the guests. To test the saying, you need some mornings with no crow, to see if guests come then too.

challenges.title: The Shelf for Everyone
challenges.problem: Your family wants a shelf for snacks that every person in the home can reach. Find the right height, without leaving anyone out.
constraints: Everyone in the home must be measured, the smallest and the tallest.
Nobody climbs on a chair or a stool to measure.
materials: a strip of paper about 2 metres long, or masking tape
a measuring tape or a ruler
general: Tape a long strip of paper on a wall, from the floor up. Each person stands flat-footed and reaches up as high as they can. Mark their reach with their name. The shelf must be no higher than the lowest mark.
Measure from the floor to each mark and write the numbers in a table.
creative: Measure also how low each person can bend comfortably, for Paati or Thatha whose knees hurt. The shelf must be between the highest low point and the lowest high point.
Ask a relative with a baby or a wheelchair user you know how high they can reach, and add them to the chart.
Make two shelves: one for the snacks children may take, and one higher up for things only grown-ups should reach, like medicines.
challenges.your_turn: Now find something else in your home that was made for one size of person. A mirror, a light switch or a hook for bags. Who is it too high or too low for?

flow.do: Ask your child what would happen if you measured only Appa's reach.
flow.say: If we measured only the tallest person and put the shelf there, who would be left out?
flow.kid: If we measured only the tallest person, who would be left out?
flow.context: This is a design challenge. You find a shelf height that everyone in your home can reach.

good: The children.
Paati, who is shorter.
Anyone smaller than Appa.

flow.do: Tape the paper strip to the wall. Measure every person's reach. Write a table: name, reach in centimetres.
flow.say: Stand flat on your feet and reach as high as you can. I'll mark it. Now the next person.
flow.kid: Stand flat. Reach up high. Mark it. Now measure everyone else.
flow.parent: Keep everyone's heels on the floor, so the test is the same for all. The youngest child's reach sets the highest the shelf can go.

flow.do: Decide the shelf height together and say who set it.
flow.say: What is the highest the shelf can be? Whose reach decided it?

challenges.title: The Check Card: stop a story before it spreads
challenges.problem: Make a small card the family can keep by the phone. It should help anyone check a message before they forward it.
constraints: It must fit on half a page.
It must use words a child of 7 can read.
It must have no more than five questions or steps.
materials: half a sheet of stiff paper or card
general: Write the three questions: Says who? How do they know? Who is missing? Add: 'If you can't answer them, don't forward it.'
Add a step: look for the source's own page, such as the weather office's website, not a copy.
creative: Draw a traffic light: red for 'no source', yellow for 'source, but no evidence', green for 'source and evidence'.
Add a question: does the message ask you to hurry, or to forward it to everyone? Real news rarely does.
Test your card on three real messages from the family phone, with a grown-up.
challenges.your_turn: Now make a check card for something else: an advert on a cereal box, a claim on a toothpaste tube, or a story a friend tells at school.
