opts: Something a famous person says
Something you can see, count or measure that shows whether a claim is true
A claim that many people repeat
How sure someone feels
quiz.why: Evidence is what you can look at or measure for yourself. A famous name, many voices or a sure feeling are not evidence.

quiz.p: Anjali's grandfather is very sure their flat has six windows. Her mother is very sure it has eight. What is the best way to find out?
opts: Believe the oldest person
Believe whoever sounds most sure
Walk round the flat and count the windows
Take a vote
quiz.why: Both of them are sure, so being sure cannot settle it. Counting the windows is evidence anyone can check.

quiz.p: In the Sure or Right? test, Kavya found that 3 of her family's 'very sure' answers were wrong. What does this show?
opts: Her family is careless
Feeling very sure does not always mean being right
Very sure answers are always wrong
The questions were unfair
quiz.why: Most very sure answers may be right, but not all. Feeling sure is a feeling. Only checking shows whether an answer is right.

quiz.p: A message says, 'NASA says the Earth will go dark for six days. Forward to everyone!' Which question should you ask first?
opts: How many people have forwarded it?
Says who? Did NASA really say it?
Is the message long?
Is it in English?
quiz.why: The message names NASA, so check NASA's own website. A message like this once went round the world, and NASA had never said it.

quiz.p: Farhan asked three friends if they like cricket. All three said yes. He says, 'All children love cricket.' What is the problem?
opts: Cricket is a boring game
Three friends is too few, and children who don't like cricket are missing
He should have asked grown-ups
Nothing, three is enough
quiz.why: He asked only three friends, who may all like the same things. The children he did not ask are missing from his evidence.

quiz.p: Meenakshi's Paati said a calling crow brings a guest. Why did she feel the saying always came true?
opts: Because crows can see guests coming
Because she remembered the days a guest came and forgot the days nobody came
Because guests only come when crows call
Because she counted every day
quiz.why: A guest is easy to remember, and an ordinary day is easy to forget. Meenakshi's tally of every day showed 9 crow days with no guest.

quiz.p: In the Top-Spoon Test, a spoonful from the top of the jar had only chana in it. But the jar also held moong at the bottom. Why was the spoonful wrong about the jar?
opts: The spoon was dirty
The sample came only from the top, so the moong was missing
Chana and moong look the same
One spoonful is always right
quiz.why: A sample tells you only about the part it came from. To learn about the whole jar, take samples from many places, or mix it first.

quiz.p: Which of these claims has been checked and found true?
opts: A goldfish forgets everything after three seconds
Lightning never strikes the same place twice
An octopus has three hearts
A camel stores water in their hump
quiz.why: Scientists have looked inside octopuses and found three hearts. The other three are repeated often, but checking has shown them wrong.

quiz.p: In 1904, Robert Wood secretly took away the prism while Prosper-René Blondlot was looking for N-rays. Blondlot kept reading out the same numbers. What did this show?
opts: N-rays can pass through anything
Blondlot was seeing what he expected, not real rays
The prism was broken
Wood was not a real scientist
quiz.why: Without the prism, the rays could not have fallen where Blondlot said. He kept seeing them because he expected to. Wood's test could have failed, and it did not.

quiz.p: Why were many scientists fooled by N-rays?
opts: They expected to see them, and the signs were faint and hard to judge
N-rays were real but disappeared later
They did not have eyes
Wood paid them
quiz.why: The rays were said to make a spark a tiny bit brighter, in a dark room. A change that small is easy to imagine when you expect it.

quiz.p: Who is usually the best source about whether it will rain in Madurai tomorrow?
opts: A message forwarded many times
The weather office, which measures air and clouds every day
Someone who is very sure
A crow on the balcony
quiz.why: The weather office measures the air across India and checks how its forecasts turned out. That is how they know.

quiz.p: Priya says, 'If a claim sounds true and lots of people say it, it must be true.' What is wrong with this?
opts: Nothing, she is right
Many claims that sound true and are repeated often turn out wrong when checked
Claims that sound true are always false
Only children repeat claims
quiz.why: The goldfish and lightning stories are repeated by many people and are wrong. What makes a claim trustworthy is that someone checked it, in a way others can repeat.

items.p: A sentence that says something is true is called a ____.
items.why: A claim can be right or wrong. Evidence shows which.

items.p: Something you can see, count or measure that shows whether a claim is true is called ____.
items.why: Counting the windows is evidence. Remembering them is weaker evidence.

items.p: Divya says, 'If someone is very sure, they must be right.' Is she right?
items.why: False. In the Sure or Right? test, some very sure answers were wrong. Being sure is a feeling, not evidence.

items.p: Revathi wants to know how many steps go up to her floor. Which is the best evidence?
opts: Her brother's guess
Counting the steps as she climbs
What she remembers from last year
Asking the oldest neighbour
items.why: Counting the steps now is evidence anyone could repeat. Guesses and memories can be wrong, even old people's.

items.p: Match each question to what it asks.
pairs: What did they do to find out?
Who or what was left out of the evidence?
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These are the three questions to ask about any claim.

items.p: Sort each claim: has it been checked and found true, or does it only sound true?
items: An octopus has three hearts.
Checked
Lightning never strikes the same place twice.
Only sounds true
Plants grow towards light.
Checked
We use only one tenth of our brain.
Only sounds true
Your heart beats faster when you run.
Checked
Bats are blind.
Only sounds true
items.a: see items
items.why: The checked claims have been tested. The others are repeated a lot but have been shown wrong.

items.p: In the Sure or Right? test, what did you find out about the answers people were very sure about? Use your own results.
items.a: A strong answer gives numbers, such as 'There were 10 very sure answers and 2 were wrong', and says what that shows.
items.why: The answer uses the child's own evidence, not a guess.

items.p: Simran asked only the grown-ups in her home if the TV was too loud. They all said no. What is missing from her evidence?
opts: The TV's brand
The children's and grandparents' answers
The time of day
Nothing
items.why: Only some people were asked. Others might find the TV too loud. Who is missing can change the answer.

items.p: Draw the jar from the Top-Spoon Test before it was mixed. Show where the spoonful came from, and label the part the spoonful missed.
items.a: A jar with two layers, a spoon at the top in the chana, and a label on the moong at the bottom saying 'missed'.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that the sample came only from the top.
items.art: A blank outline of a tall jar and a spoon.

items.p: Arun says, 'A whispered message stays the same however many people pass it on.' Is he right?
items.why: False. In the Passing Message, the words changed as they went along. Each person can add, drop or change a little.

items.p: Three of these are good evidence. Which one is the odd one out?
opts: Counting the windows yourself
A photo of the plant taken every day
A message that says 'everyone knows this'
A table written during the test
items.why: 'Everyone knows this' gives no source and no evidence. The others can be checked.

items.p: Why did Meenakshi say they must write down the boring days, when no guest came?
items.a: Because the boring days are the ones people forget. Without them, every guest seems to come on a crow day. Writing every day shows the misses as well as the hits.
items.why: A strong answer says that people remember hits and forget misses.

items.p: Two sisters in Kochi argue about the old saying that a crow calling means a guest is coming.

views.says: Paati has seen it happen many times. She is old and wise, so the saying must be true.
Paati is wise, but she might remember only the days it worked. We should write down every day for a week and count.

items.ask: Which sister do you agree with more? Give a reason. Then say one thing the other sister has right.
items.a: A strong answer sees that a tally of every day is better evidence than memory. It also gives Lakshmi her due: Paati has watched crows for years, and she noticed something true, that crows call a lot.
items.why: Pick-a-side questions have no single right answer. Marks go for using evidence and stating the other view fairly.

items.p: Put the steps of checking a claim in order.
items: Look at the real thing, or ask someone who measured it
Hear the claim
Decide if the claim is right
Ask: says who, and how do they know?
a: Ask: says who, and how do they know?
Look at the real thing, or ask someone who measured it
Decide if the claim is right
items.why: You decide last, after you have asked the questions and looked at the evidence.

items.p: Here is a forwarded message: 'Doctors say eating three bananas a day makes you taller. My cousin tried it! Forward to everyone.' Label the part with no named source, the part that is only one person's story, and the part that rushes you.
items.a: No named source: 'Doctors say'. Only one person's story: 'My cousin tried it'. Rushes you: 'Forward to everyone'.
items.why: A strong answer finds all three parts and says why each one is a warning sign.
items.art: A phone screen showing the message, with three empty label boxes and arrows.

items.p: Mehak kept a tally for 10 mornings. A crow called on all 10. A guest came on 3. Can she say the crow brings guests?
opts: Yes, three guests came on crow days
No. The crow called every day, so she has no quiet days to compare
Yes, because three is more than none
No, because crows never call
items.why: If the sign is there every day, every guest comes on a sign day. To test the saying, she needs some days with no crow, to see if guests come then too.

items.p: Paati said a crow calling means a guest is coming. What result in a tally would make you think the saying might be true?
items.a: Guests coming on many of the crow days, and hardly ever on the days with no crow, over many weeks.
items.why: A strong answer compares crow days with no-crow days, and wants many days, not a few.

items.p: Tanvi says, 'Asking who is missing means the evidence is useless.' Is she right?
items.why: False. It means the evidence tells you about the people who were asked, not about everyone. You can then go and ask the missing people.

items.p: For many years, most crash tests for cars used a dummy the size of an average man. Explain why this could make cars less safe for some people.
items.a: People of other sizes, such as many women and older children, sit differently and are hurt in different ways. If they were missing from the tests, the car was not made safe for their bodies.
items.why: A strong answer says who was missing and how that changes what the test can tell us.

items.p: In the Be Clever Hans activity, the tapper did well when the watching grown-up knew the answer, and badly when nobody watching knew it. What does this tell us about Clever Hans the horse?
opts: Hans did the sums in his head
Hans read tiny signs from the people watching him
Hans was not trying
Hans could read numbers on paper
items.why: If Hans had done the sums, it would not have mattered who knew the answer. He was reading faces and bodies, which is a real skill of its own.

items.p: Sort each source: did they see or measure it themselves, or did they hear it from someone else?
items: A doctor who looked at your throat
Saw or measured
A cousin who read a message
Heard from someone
The weather office's rain gauge
Saw or measured
A friend whose friend was there
Heard from someone
Your tally from this morning
Saw or measured
A message that says 'scientists say'
Heard from someone
items.a: see items
items.why: A source who saw or measured it is closer to what happened. Every time a claim is passed on, it can change.

items.p: Two friends in Hyderabad read a claim on a cereal box: 'Children who eat this cereal do better at school.'

views.says: It's printed on the box, so it must be checked. Companies aren't allowed to lie.
Says who? The company wants to sell cereal. And children who eat breakfast might do better anyway, whatever they eat.

items.ask: Which friend do you agree with more? Use the three questions in your answer. Then say one thing the other friend has right.
items.a: A strong answer asks who tested it, how, and against what. It also gives Anjali her due: there are rules about what can be printed on food packets.
items.why: Marks go for using the three questions, and for stating the other view fairly.

items.p: Draw a tally chart with four boxes for the Crow and Guest Week: crow and guest, crow and no guest, no crow and guest, no crow and no guest. Fill it in with made-up numbers that would show the saying is wrong.
items.a: Any numbers where guests come about as often on no-crow days as on crow days, for example 2 out of 5 crow days and 2 out of 5 no-crow days.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that guests come just as often with or without the crow.
items.art: A blank 2 by 2 grid with row labels 'Crow' and 'No crow' and column labels 'Guest' and 'No guest'.

items.p: The part of something you look at, to learn about the whole thing, is called a ____.
items.why: One spoonful from the dal jar is a sample. A sample tells you only about the part it came from.

items.p: Match each claim to the best way to check it.
pairs: Keep a tally for a week
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: The best check depends on the claim. Some you look at, some you measure over time, and some only one person can answer.

items.p: Robert Wood removed the prism without telling Blondlot. Why was it important that Blondlot did not know?
items.a: If Blondlot had known, he would have expected to see nothing, and he would have reported nothing whether the rays were real or not. Not knowing meant only the rays could decide what he saw.
items.why: A strong answer says that what we expect can change what we think we see.

items.p: Three of these are reasons a story can seem true when it is not. Which is the odd one out?
opts: People remember the hits and forget the misses
Many people repeat it
It was tested and the result was repeated by others
A famous name is attached to it
items.why: A test that others repeated with the same result is a reason to trust a claim. The other three can make a story seem true without any evidence.

items.p: Ishita's aunt has a cold. She drinks ginger tea, and two days later the cold is gone. Why is this not good evidence that ginger tea cures colds?
opts: Ginger is not a plant
Colds usually go away in a few days anyway, so one person's story shows nothing
Tea is always bad for colds
Two days is too long
items.why: Most colds get better by themselves. To know if the tea helped, you would need to compare many people who drank it with many who did not.

items.p: Here is a results table from a Sure or Right? test. Label the column that is a feeling, and the column that is evidence.
items.a: The 'How sure' column is a feeling. The 'Right or wrong, after checking' column is evidence.
items.why: How sure people felt was a feeling inside them. Checking the real thing gave the evidence.
items.art: A results table with columns Question, Person, Answer, How sure, Right or wrong after checking, and two empty label boxes.

items.p: Your friend says, 'I don't trust anything anyone tells me.' Is that a good way to think? Explain.
items.a: Not quite. We cannot check everything ourselves, so we need to trust some people. The point is to trust them because of how they know, and to check when we can.
items.why: A strong answer says that 'says who?' is not the same as trusting nobody.

items.p: Plan a test of a saying from your own family, such as 'an itchy palm means money is coming'. What will you write down every day, and why must you decide the rules first?
items.a: Write down every day whether the sign happened and whether the result came. Decide the rules first, because if you decide afterwards it is easy to count things that fit the saying.
items.why: A strong plan records every day, names the rules, and has days with and without the sign.

items.p: In the Sure or Right? test, Kavya's family gave 12 'very sure' answers, and 3 were wrong. They gave 10 'just guessing' answers, and 5 were wrong. What is the fairest conclusion?
opts: Being sure is useless
Very sure answers were right more often than guesses, but some were still wrong
Guessing is better than being sure
The test was unfair
items.why: 9 of 12 very sure answers were right, and 5 of 10 guesses were right. So being sure often goes with being right, but it is not proof.

items.p: Three people talk about the N-rays story.

views.says: The N-rays story shows that science works. A scientist tested the claim and caught the mistake within about a year.
The story shows that even scientists see what they expect. Dozens of them were fooled.
The story shows we should always test claims in ways that could fail, like taking away the prism.

items.ask: Which person do you agree with most? Can two of them be right at once? Explain.
items.a: A strong answer sees that all three have a point. Scientists can be fooled, and science also has ways to catch it, if someone tests in a way that could fail.
items.why: Real stories can teach more than one lesson. Marks go for reasons and for being fair to the other views.

items.p: Karl Popper said a claim is scientific if a test could show it is wrong. Is 'A crow calling brings a guest' scientific by his idea? Is 'Everything happens for a reason'? Explain both.
items.a: The crow claim is, because a tally could show guests come no more often on crow days. 'Everything happens for a reason' is hard to test, because any result could be said to fit it.
items.why: A strong answer says what result would show each claim wrong, or says that none could.

items.p: Some old remedies have been tested. Tu Youyou, a scientist in China, read about sweet wormwood in a book about 1,700 years old. Tests showed a substance in it treats malaria. What does this show?
opts: All old remedies work
All old remedies are just stories
Old knowledge should be tested, and some of it passes
Only Chinese books are right
items.why: Some old knowledge is right and some is wrong. The fair thing is to test each one, not to decide in advance.

items.p: Draw a cartoon in three boxes showing how a true message could turn false as it is passed on. Show who first saw what happened.
items.a: Three boxes: someone sees something and tells a friend, the friend passes it on with a change, and the last person tells a very different story.
items.why: A strong cartoon shows the first person was there, and that each passing can change the message.
items.art: Three empty cartoon boxes in a row.

items.p: Nila says, 'If a test of a claim could never come out wrong, the test tells us nothing.' Is she right?
items.why: True. If every result would fit the claim, the test cannot tell us whether the claim is right. Wood's prism test was strong because it could have shown the rays were real.

items.p: A new medicine is tested only on adults. A doctor wants to give it to a child of 7. What question should she ask, and why?
items.a: Who is missing? Children were not in the test. A child's body is smaller and can respond to medicines differently, so she needs evidence from tests on children.
items.why: A strong answer names the missing group and says why it matters.

items.p: Sort each statement: is it a claim you can check, or a feeling or a taste that belongs to a person?
items: Our flat has seven windows.
Claim you can check
Mango is the best fruit.
A person's feeling or taste
The milk packet says 'Toned'.
Claim you can check
Rainy days are the nicest days.
A person's feeling or taste
Water boils sooner with a lid on the pan.
Claim you can check
Pongal is my favourite festival.
A person's feeling or taste
items.a: see items
items.why: Some sentences can be checked by anyone. Others tell you about the person who said them, and only that person can answer.

items.p: In the Top-Spoon Test, after mixing, three spoonfuls had 20, 23 and 18 moong grains. Why are the numbers not all the same?
opts: The test went wrong
Each spoonful is a small sample, and samples differ a little by chance
Moong grains change size
Only the first spoon counts
items.why: Even in a well-mixed jar, each spoonful takes a slightly different set of grains. That is why scientists take several samples and look at all of them.

items.p: Pfungst found Clever Hans read tiny signs from people. Does that mean Hans was not clever? Explain your view.
items.a: A strong answer says Hans did not do sums, but he was very good at noticing tiny changes in people's faces and bodies, better than most humans. He was clever in a different way from the one people claimed.
items.why: A good answer separates the claim that was wrong (Hans did sums) from what Hans really could do.

items.p: Put Robert Wood's N-rays test in the order it happened.
items: Blondlot kept reading out the same numbers
Wood quietly took the prism away in the dark
Wood wrote up what happened in the journal Nature
Blondlot said he saw N-rays spread out by a prism
a: Blondlot said he saw N-rays spread out by a prism
Wood quietly took the prism away in the dark
Blondlot kept reading out the same numbers
Wood wrote up what happened in the journal Nature
items.why: First the claim, then the test that could fail, then the result, then sharing it so others could judge.

items.p: Match each mistake to the story or test that showed it.
pairs: Seeing what you expect to see
Leaving a group out of the evidence
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each story shows a different way evidence can go wrong.

items.p: Here is Meenakshi's two-week tally from the story Paati's Crow: crow and guest 4, crow and no guest 9, no crow and guest 0, no crow and no guest 1. Label the box Paati remembered, and the box she forgot.
items.a: Remembered: crow and guest (4). Forgot: crow and no guest (9).
items.why: The hits were remembered and the misses forgotten. The no-crow boxes are too small to tell anything, because there was only one quiet day.
items.art: A 2 by 2 grid with the four numbers filled in and two empty labels.

items.p: Write one claim you heard this week. Answer the three questions about it: Says who? How do they know? Who is missing?
items.a: A strong answer names a real claim, gives a source, says what evidence exists or is missing, and names a group or part left out.
items.why: This uses all three questions on something from the child's own life.

applications: Doctors ask who was in a medicine's tests before they give it to a child, a pregnant woman or an old person.
Journalists check a story with a second source before they print it.
Fact-checkers trace a forwarded message back to where it started.
Judges and police know that a witness can be sure and still wrong, so they look for other evidence too.
Car makers now test seats with dummies of different sizes.
Scientists hide which sample is which from the person measuring, so expectations cannot change what they see.
Survey makers try to ask people from every group, not only the people easiest to reach.

open_questions.q: Why do people feel sure about some memories that are wrong?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know that memories are rebuilt each time we recall them, and can change. Nobody fully knows why a wrong memory can feel just as sure as a right one.

open_questions.q: How much should we trust experts when they disagree?
open_questions.why_open: Philosophers and scientists still argue about this. There is no simple rule that works every time.

open_questions.q: Can any test be completely free of what the tester expects?
open_questions.why_open: Hiding information from testers, as Wood did, helps a lot. But scientists still argue about how far expectations creep into what we choose to measure.

open_questions.q: Why do false stories often spread faster than true ones?
open_questions.why_open: Some studies of social media found that false news spread further and faster than true news. Researchers are still working out why, and whether it is true everywhere.

maths.problem: In Kavya's Sure or Right? test, her family gave 12 'very sure' answers. 3 were wrong. How many were right?
maths.explain: 12 take away 3 is 9. So 9 of the 12 very sure answers were right, and 3 were wrong.
maths.context: This is about Sure or Right?, where you ask your family questions about your home and check the answers.
maths.why_maths: Counting the right and the wrong answers turns a feeling ('they're usually right') into evidence.

maths.problem: Kavya's family gave 10 'just guessing' answers, and 5 were right. They gave 12 'very sure' answers, and 9 were right. Which kind of answer was right more often?
maths.answer: The very sure answers. 9 out of 12 is more than half. 5 out of 10 is exactly half.
maths.explain: Half of 12 is 6, and 9 is more than 6. Half of 10 is 5, so the guesses were right exactly half the time. Very sure answers did better, but not perfectly.
maths.context: This is about Sure or Right?, where you ask your family questions about your home and check the answers.
maths.why_maths: Comparing each group with a half lets you compare two groups of different sizes fairly.

maths.problem: In the story Paati's Crow, a crow called on 13 mornings. A guest came on 4 of those days. On how many crow days did nobody come?
maths.explain: 13 take away 4 is 9. Paati remembered the 4 days and forgot the 9.
maths.context: This is about the story Paati's Crow, where Meenakshi keeps a tally to test a saying about crows and guests.
maths.why_maths: Counting the misses as well as the hits is how a tally catches a saying that only sounds true.

maths.problem: Divya plays One True, One Made Up with 10 pairs of claims. If she only guesses, about how many will she get right?
maths.explain: Each pair has two choices, so a guess is right about half the time. Half of 10 is 5. If she gets 9 or 10 right, she probably knows something.
maths.context: This is about One True, One Made Up, where a grown-up says two claims and you pick the true one.
maths.why_maths: Knowing what guessing would give tells you whether a good score shows real knowledge or luck.

maths.problem: In the Top-Spoon Test after mixing, three spoonfuls had 20, 23 and 18 moong grains. What is the total? What is the difference between the biggest and the smallest?
maths.answer: The total is 61. The difference is 5.
maths.explain: 20 + 23 + 18 = 61. The biggest is 23 and the smallest is 18. 23 take away 18 is 5. The spoonfuls are close, but not the same, so one spoonful alone could mislead a little.
maths.context: This is about the Top-Spoon Test, where you take spoonfuls from a jar of two kinds of dal.
maths.why_maths: The difference between samples shows how much one sample can vary by chance.

roots.context: We have tested how often people are sure and wrong, and learned to ask: says who, how do they know, and who is missing? Now we ask what this tells us about knowing anything at all.

deep_truth.truth: Some answers your family gave as 'very sure' were wrong when you checked the real thing. Being sure is a feeling inside the person. The clock on the wall stays the same, however sure anyone feels. So how sure someone sounds tells you about them, and only checking tells you about the clock.
deep_truth.habit: We treat a sure voice as if it were proof, our own most of all. But the feeling of being sure comes from memory and habit, which can drift away from the thing itself. The test showed the two can come apart.
deep_truth.evidence: In Sure or Right?, every person answered from memory and said how sure they were. Then the family looked at the clock, the windows and the tap. Some very sure answers did not match what was there.

three.who_am_i: You are someone who can feel sure and be wrong. You are also someone who can notice it and check.
three.what_is_life: Every living thing acts on what they sense and remember. A crow comes back each morning to the balcony where rice was put out before, and looks to see if there is more.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is the same whatever anyone believes about it. That is why two people who check carefully end up agreeing.

roots.thread: Each person in your home carries their own picture of the flat in their memory. The pictures differ a little, and each one feels sure. But there is only one flat, and when everyone goes and looks, the pictures come together. Many views, one world: checking is how the many come back to the one.

teachings.teaching: The Buddha told the Kalama people not to accept a teaching only because it is repeated, or written in a book, or because the teacher is respected. When you know for yourselves that it is true and good, then accept it.
teachings.link: Paati was respected and the crow saying was old and often repeated. Meenakshi did what the Buddha advised: she found out for herself, with a tally.

teachings.source: Jain anekantavada, many-sidedness, and the story of the blind men and the elephant
teachings.teaching: Several blind men touch one elephant. One feels the trunk and says it is a snake. One feels a leg and says it is a pillar. Each is sure, and each has only a part.
teachings.link: In the Top-Spoon Test, the top spoonful was sure the jar was all chana. It had only a part. Asking 'who is missing?' is asking what part of the elephant we have not touched.

science.text: Memories are rebuilt each time we recall them, so a memory can change and still feel sure.
Scientists hide which sample is which from the people measuring, because expectations can change what people see, as in the N-rays story.

other_view.who: Philosophers who study trust, such as many in the tradition of Thomas Reid
other_view.view: Most of what anyone knows comes from what others told us, and we could not live if we checked it all. Trusting what people say is the normal way of knowing, and doubting should be kept for when there is a reason to doubt.

practice.title: Sure, then look
practice.say: Close your eyes. Think of the door of this room. Is the handle on the left or the right? Say how sure you are. Now open your eyes and look. Were you right? Close your eyes again. Feel the floor under you. You don't need to remember the floor. It is right here. Open your eyes slowly.

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if in a city flat, with the materials listed. Sure or Right? needs at least two people besides the child, so the steps offer a phone call to relatives, who answer about their own home and check while on the call. Eight questions about the home, with a mix of easy and hard ones, nearly always give at least one confident wrong answer, because people rarely look closely at clocks, taps and stairs. If every very sure answer is right, the steps say to add three harder questions. Counting stairs is done with a grown-up. The Top-Spoon Test uses chana over green moong (any big pale grain over any small dark one), with at least 3 centimetres of each. The layers show clearly through a clear jar. Mixing is done by hand on a plate, because shaking a jar tends to bring big grains back to the top. Be Clever Hans works best with a third person to pick the sums, and the steps give a shuffled-slip version for two. The Crow and Guest Week works in most Indian cities, where house crows call every day. If no crow is heard, the steps suggest testing another family saying. The spine (intro, One True One Made Up, Sure or Right?, the explanation cards, how we found out, roots and quiz) fits about 85 minutes in two sessions.

how_we_found_out.story: In 1903, Prosper-René Blondlot, a respected physicist at the University of Nancy in France, announced a new kind of invisible ray. He called them N-rays, after his city. He said they made a tiny electric spark glow a little brighter. Dozens of other scientists, mostly in France, soon reported seeing N-rays too. But scientists in other countries tried and saw nothing. In 1904, the American physicist Robert Wood visited Blondlot's lab. Blondlot used a prism, a block that bends rays, to spread the N-rays out, and he read off where each one fell. The room was dark. While Blondlot worked, Wood quietly took the prism away. Blondlot kept reading out the same numbers, as if nothing had changed. The rays he saw were not there. He had seen what he expected to see. Wood wrote up what happened in the journal Nature that September, and within a few years almost nobody spoke of N-rays again.
how_we_found_out.who: Prosper-René Blondlot, a French physicist, and Robert Wood, an American physicist who tested his claim
how_we_found_out.when: 1903 (N-rays announced), 1904 (Wood's visit to Nancy and his report in Nature)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Many scientists believed N-rays were real, because a respected physicist and many others said they saw them. Wood's test, removing the prism without telling anyone, showed that the rays were seen even when they could not be there.
